**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me, *"You’re not trying hard enough."* I was eight, sitting at the kitchen table with a math worksheet smeared with eraser dust. The numbers blurred together, and my fingers ached from gripping the pencil too tight. His voice wasn’t loud—it didn’t need to be. The words settled in my stomach like a stone.

I didn’t know then that some sentences are boulders, that they roll through years, gathering moss, cracking ribs. I didn’t know that *"you’re not trying hard enough"* would become the chorus of my inner monologue, humming beneath every failure, every half-finished project, every time I hesitated.

Words are supposed to be light, aren’t they? They float on breath, dissolve into air. But some linger. Some carve grooves into your bones.

---

II.

I once read that the average person speaks about 16,000 words a day. That’s 16,000 chances to build or break, to mend or maim. Most of them are forgettable—*"pass the salt," "what time is it?"*—but some stick like burrs.

My mother used to say, *"You have a face like a storm cloud."* She meant it affectionately, or at least I think she did. But I started checking my reflection obsessively, tilting my head to see if my eyebrows really did sag like rain-heavy skies. I practiced smiling in the mirror until my cheeks hurt.

Words shape us before we even know we’re being shaped.

---

III.

There’s a myth that Eskimos have fifty words for snow. (It’s not true, or at least not in the way we think—it’s more about how language adapts to necessity.) But I like the idea. That a people could look at something so ordinary, so ever-present, and find fifty ways to describe its nuances. *Powder. Slush. Drift. Crust.* Each word a different texture underfoot.

What if we did that with emotions? What if we had fifty words for grief, or fifty for love? Instead of *"I’m sad,"* we could say, *"My heart is a bruised peach,"* or *"I am the hollow after a scream."* Language could be a scalpel, precise enough to cut to the truth.

But we don’t. We say *"I’m fine"* when we mean *"I am drowning."* We say *"I love you"* when we mean *"Don’t leave me."* We use words like blunt instruments, and then we’re surprised when they leave scars.

---

IV.

I had a professor in college who believed silence was the most powerful form of communication. He’d stand at the front of the lecture hall, arms crossed, and wait. Someone would raise a hand. He’d nod, but say nothing. The silence would stretch, thick and suffocating, until the student’s voice cracked under the pressure.

*"Why aren’t you answering?"* someone asked once.

*"Because,"* he said, *"the right words are worth waiting for."*

I thought of him years later, when I was sitting across from my best friend in a diner at 3 a.m. She’d just been diagnosed with something unpronounceable, something that would require chemotherapy and a wig and a kind of bravery I couldn’t fathom. I opened my mouth, and nothing came out. Not *"it’ll be okay"* (a lie), not *"I’m so sorry"* (useless), not *"I love you"* (true, but not enough).

I reached across the table and took her hand. She squeezed back. Sometimes, the right words don’t exist.

---

V.

The internet has made us fluent in outrage. We wield words like weapons, firing them into the void, hoping they’ll wound someone, anyone. *"Cancel him."* *"She’s a monster."* *"Burn it all down."* We type in caps lock, as if volume equals truth.

But outrage is exhausting. It’s a fire that consumes everything, including the person holding the match. I’ve said things I didn’t mean because anger felt like power. I’ve watched friendships crumble over a poorly phrased tweet. Words, once released, can’t be unsaid. They echo.

I wonder sometimes if we’ve forgotten how to speak softly. How to say, *"I disagree, but I still respect you."* How to admit, *"I don’t know."* How to listen.

---

VI.

My grandmother had Alzheimer’s. Toward the end, her words became a puzzle—fragments of sentences, half-remembered names, sudden bursts of clarity like sunlight through storm clouds. One afternoon, she looked at me and said, *"You have your father’s eyes. But you got your heart from me."*

I didn’t know what to say. So I just held her hand.

A week later, she forgot my name. Then she forgot how to speak at all. The last time I saw her, she was humming a tune I didn’t recognize. No words, just sound. Maybe that’s all we are, in the end—vibrations in the air, brief and beautiful and gone too soon.

---

VII.

I write because words are the only way I know how to make sense of the chaos. When my anxiety spirals, I spill it onto the page, and suddenly, it’s not inside me anymore. When I’m in love, I write odes to freckles and the way someone laughs with their whole body. When I’m grieving, I write until my fingers cramp.

But writing is also a lie. It’s the illusion of control. You can arrange words just so, craft the perfect sentence, and still, life will not bend to your narrative. People will still leave. Bodies will still fail. The world will still be cruel and beautiful in equal measure.

And yet. And yet.

There is power in naming things. In saying, *"This hurt me."* In whispering, *"I am here."* In shouting, *"I will not be erased!"*

Words are not just sounds. They are bridges. They are bombs. They are balm.

---

VIII.

If I had 1,000 words to say anything, I’d tell you this:

Life is short, and words are long. They outlive us. They echo in the people we’ve loved, the strangers we’ve hurt, the children who repeat what we’ve said without thinking. So choose them carefully. Say *"I love you"* like you mean it. Say *"I’m sorry"* even when it’s hard. Say *"I don’t know"* when you don’t. Say *"You matter"* to someone who needs to hear it.

And sometimes, say nothing at all. Just be there. Hold a hand. Share the silence.

The world is loud enough.

---
*(998 words. I saved two for the things we haven’t said yet.)*
